new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexically/morphologically governed rather than positional: roots are lexically 'strong' or 'weak'; a strong root keeps the stress, while with a weak root the stress falls on a (strong) suffix, including lexical suffixes such as =éyus 'pants' or =(m)éix 'house'. Koch attributes the strong/weak root analysis to Thompson & Thompson 1992, whose own formulation (with the full suffix hierarchy) was not opened.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the opened sources.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress does not shift under narrow focus: a focused unstressed root (keʔɬ- 'three') stays unstressed while the lexical suffix =éyus 'pants' keeps the word stress; a focused unstressed lexical suffix (=kst 'hand') does not attract stress from the stressed root ləx-lix. English loan nouns (Péter, tiy 'tea') stress the lexical content, often an open syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (word-level stress marked with acute accent in T&T orthography); Koch's own study concerns phrase-level nuclear stress, which he finds rightmost in the clause. Koch's data are from two speakers of the Lytton (ƛ'q'əmcín) dialect; the phonemic description he adopts (T&T 1992) is based on the Spuzzum dialect.
new_statements.identity_note: Sources describe Nɬeʔkepmxcín (Thompson River Salish) = thom1243. Koch 2008 data come from the Lytton (ƛ'q'əmcín) dialect; Thompson & Thompson 1992, the description Koch relies on, is based on the Spuzzum dialect. No separate Glottolog dialect codes assigned here.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for thom1243 has an empty rule; the one existing statement (Koch 2008) reads the system as morphologically determined with strong/weak roots and stress on functional suffixes, citing Thompson & Thompson 1992. Jimmie agrees that stress is a strong/weak morpheme system (same source, T&T 1992) and adds the explicit rule text (22a), her own rightmost-stressable-element formulation (25), cyclicity, secondary stress on out-competed morphemes, the prefix and syllabic-nasal exclusions, and the reduplication exception. One point of tension: Koch says 'in the default case, the leftmost lexical stress surfaces', whereas Jimmie (after T&T) says that with two underlyingly stressed syl…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is not positionally fixed; it is determined by the lexical strong/weak (stressable/non-stressable) status of the morphemes in the word. Rule (22a), which Jimmie takes from Thompson & Thompson (1992:22): main stress falls on a strong morpheme; failing that, on the first suffix that can take stress; failing that, on the root. Prefixes and vowelless morphemes never bear stress. Jimmie's own preliminary rule (25), modelled on Czaykowska-Higgins (1993b) for Columbian: assign stress to the rightmost stressable element, except that a strong root keeps the stress unless there is more than one lexical suffix or the lexical suffix is itself strong; a strong suffix keeps it unless more than two suffixes follow, in which case the rightmost suffix is stressed. Stress assignment is cyclic (pp. 19-20); with two underlyingly stressed syllables in a derived form, the last one gets main stress (p. 16). She stresses that 'there are irregularities in stress assignment' (p. 18): stress sometimes falls on the root, sometimes on the first or the last suffix, sometimes on internal non-final suffixes.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 16: 'They further state that other morphemes are unstressed or have secondary stress. [..] Other morphemes are underlyingly assigned secondary stress; therefore they never have primary stress.' pp. 16-17: 'if a derived form has two underlyingly stressed syllable[s] stress falls on the last stressed syllable, and the previously underlying stressed syllable will now have secondary stress, which will be deleted at a later stage.' (Reported from Thompson & Thompson 1992, no acoustic evidence given.)
new_statements.exceptions: Prefixes never take stress (p. 16 rule 22a; p. 17 fn. 14: 'prefixes never have stress assigned to them'); morphemes without a vowel cannot take stress (p. 16); 'only vowels are stressed; syllabic nasals are never stressed' (p. 26); weak roots yield stress to any suffix with an underlying vowel, and lexical + inflectional suffix combinations show further irregularities (p. 18); unstressed vowels delete unless followed by more than one consonant before the main stress (rule 22b, p. 16); augmentative reduplication is exceptional in that 'stress shifts leftward onto the reduplicated prefix' (p. 72).
new_statements.identity_note: Jimmie 1994 describes Nɬeʔkepmx (Thompson-Salish) as a whole, drawing her data mainly from Thompson & Thompson 1992 and from her own knowledge as a speaker (Nlaka'pamux); no dialect is singled out. Section 1.3.2 summarises Czaykowska-Higgins (1993b) on Nxaʔamxcin (Columbian Salish, a different language) only as a theoretical model, not as data on Thompson.

readall_conflicts: One apparent disagreement on the tie-break direction: Koch 2008 (existing statement, p. 166) says 'in the default case, the leftmost lexical stress surfaces on a verb', while Jimmie 1994 pp. 16 and 20, following Thompson & Thompson 1992, says main stress goes to the last of two underlyingly stressed syllables and her preliminary rule assigns stress to the rightmost stressable element (strong root wins only when at most one, non-strong lexical suffix follows). Both sources agree on the core: stress is governed by lexically marked strong/weak roots and suffixes, prefixes are never stressed, and a weak root cedes stress to a stressable suffix. The primary source both cite, Thompson & Thompson 1992 (UMOPL 8), is still not obtainable online, so the direction of the default cannot be settled from what was opened; Jimmie herself calls her rule 'a very preliminary analysis' (p. 19) and notes irregularities (p. 18).
